phy_ocrb.7.3.summary: These revision notes cover PAG7 (Series and parallel circuits) and PAG8 (Interactions of waves) for OCR GCSE Physics B. You must master how to safely set up electrical circuits to investigate current, potential difference, and resistance, alongside experimental methods for measuring wave speed, frequency, and wavelength in both tanks and solids. Expect rigorous questions on controlling variables, calculating uncertainties, sketching circuit diagrams, and analyzing wave phenomena using standard apparatus.

core.h: PAG7: Designing and Setting Up Electrical Circuits
core.p: Practical Activity Group 7 requires you to construct series and parallel circuits using standard circuit symbols, select appropriate meters, and take accurate measurements to determine resistance or investigate current-voltage relationships.
bullets: Use a power supply, ammeters, voltmeters, variable resistors, switches, and component holders.
Always connect ammeters in series with the component through which the current is being measured.
Always connect voltmeters in parallel across the component across which the potential difference is being measured.
Check all circuit connections before turning on the power supply to prevent short circuits or component damage.

callouts.p: Ammeters have very low resistance and must never be connected in parallel across a supply. Voltmeters have very high resistance and must be placed in parallel.

core.p: In a series circuit, components are connected in a single loop. You must investigate how current and potential difference behave across multiple components.
bullets: The current is the same at all points in a single closed series loop: I1 = I2 = I3.
The total potential difference of the power supply is shared between the components in a series circuit: V_total = V1 + V2 + V3.
Adding more resistors in series increases the total resistance of the circuit, thereby decreasing the total current.
If one component in a series circuit breaks or is disconnected, the complete circuit is broken and current stops flowing everywhere.

callouts.p: In a series circuit, the sum of the potential differences across each component equals the total potential difference of the power supply.

core.p: In a parallel circuit, components are connected across multiple branches. You must verify how current splits and potential difference remains constant across each parallel branch.
bullets: The potential difference across each parallel branch is the same and equals the source potential difference: V_source = V1 = V2.
The total current entering a junction splits between the branches: I_total = I1 + I2 + I3.
Adding more resistors in parallel provides alternative paths for charge flow, which decreases the total resistance of the circuit.
If one branch in a parallel circuit is disconnected, the other branches continue to operate normally.

callouts.p: When describing parallel circuits, always refer to junctions and branches using Kirchhoff's first idea without necessarily naming it.

core.h: PAG7: Resistance Calculations and IV Characteristics
core.p: You must use experimental data of current and potential difference to calculate resistance using Ohm's Law and investigate non-ohmic components.
bullets: Calculate resistance using the formula R = V / I, where R is in ohms (Ω), V is in volts (V), and I is in amperes (A).
Plot graphs of current against potential difference to analyze component behavior.
An ohmic conductor has a constant straight-line graph passing through the origin at constant temperature.
Filament lamps and diodes show non-linear IV characteristics due to changing temperature or direction-dependent resistance.

callouts.p: Leaving the current switched on too long during resistance experiments causes components to heat up, changing their resistance and ruining data accuracy.

core.h: PAG8: Measuring Wave Speed in Solids
core.p: PAG8 requires you to measure the speed of waves using appropriate methods, including standing waves in solids or traveling waves.
bullets: For a stretched metal wire or rod, support it securely and strike or vibrate it to produce a standing wave.
Measure the length L of the vibrating section and identify nodes and antinodes to determine wavelength lambda.
Calculate wave speed using the wave equation v = f * lambda, where f is the known frequency of the signal generator.
Alternatively, measure the time taken for a transverse pulse to travel along a solid bar or tensioned string of known length.

callouts.p: Measure across multiple wavelengths rather than just one to reduce percentage error in wavelength determination.

core.h: PAG8: Ripple Tank Waves and Frequency
core.p: Ripple tanks are standard apparatus used to observe water wave properties, measure wavelength, frequency, and wave speed.
bullets: Illuminate the ripple tank from above so that wave crests project as bright lines on a white sheet of paper below.
Measure the wavelength by taking a photograph with a ruler in view or freezing the pattern using a stroboscope.
Determine the frequency by counting the number of wave crests passing a fixed point per unit time using a stopwatch.
Calculate wave speed using v = f * lambda and compare it with direct timing methods over a known distance.

callouts.p: Adjust the stroboscope frequency until the waves appear stationary to easily measure their apparent wavelength.

core.p: You must investigate the reflection of waves using ripple tanks or light rays, verifying the law of reflection.
bullets: Set up plane waves in a ripple tank and place a flat barrier in their path at an angle.
Observe how the wavefronts reflect off the barrier, maintaining the same angle relative to the normal.
The angle of incidence i is always equal to the angle of reflection r.
Measure angles using a protractor perpendicular to the reflecting barrier.

callouts.p: The angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection, measured from the normal.

core.p: Refraction occurs when waves change speed as they pass from one medium into another of different density or depth.
bullets: In a ripple tank, place a transparent glass plate underneath the water to create a shallow region.
As waves pass from deep water into shallow water, their speed decreases and their wavelength decreases.
The frequency of the waves remains constant because it is determined by the source.
If waves enter the shallow region at an angle to the boundary, the wavefronts change direction (refract).

callouts.p: Never state that frequency changes during refraction. Frequency is strictly constant across the boundary.

core.p: Diffraction is the spreading out of waves when they pass through a gap or around an obstacle.
bullets: In a ripple tank, create obstacles with gaps of varying widths.
Maximum diffraction occurs when the size of the gap is equal to or smaller than the wavelength of the waves.
When the gap is much larger than the wavelength, little diffraction occurs, and straight wavefronts pass through with shadowed edges.
Obstacles also cause diffraction, creating shadow regions behind them.

callouts.p: Maximum spreading (diffraction) is observed when the aperture width is approximately equal to the incident wavelength.

core.p: Both PAG7 and PAG8 require rigorous evaluation of random and systematic errors, precision improvements, and adherence to electrical or water safety protocols.
bullets: Identify random errors such as parallax error when reading meters or rulers, and reduce them by taking repeated readings and calculating means.
Identify systematic errors such as zero errors on ammeters, voltmeters, or stopwatches; correct them before recording data.
In PAG7, prevent overheating by turning off power supplies between readings or using low currents.
In PAG8, ensure electrical equipment near ripple tanks is protected against water splashes and residual moisture.

callouts.p: Always state explicitly that you checked the meter needle or digital readout pointed to zero before starting measurements.

analogy.t: The Water Supply and Obstacle Course Analogy
analogy.p: Think of a series circuit as a single narrow water pipe where every water wheel must be turned by the same flow of water. A parallel circuit is like a river splitting into multiple channels around an island, where the water splits and recombines. For waves, think of marching soldiers hitting a muddy patch (refraction) where they slow down and turn, or walking through a narrow doorway (diffraction) where they spread out into the room. This breaks down because electrons in circuits carry energy through potential differences, whereas water waves transport momentum and energy through mechanical oscillations without net transfer of matter.

terms.d: A circuit in which all components are connected in a single closed loop so the same current flows through each.
A circuit with multiple branches, allowing current to split and flow through alternative paths independently.
Work done per unit charge flowing between two points in a circuit, measured in volts.
The rate of flow of electrical charge past a point in a circuit, measured in amperes.
A measure of how difficult it is for current to flow through a component, measured in ohms.
States that current is directly proportional to potential difference across a conductor at constant temperature.
A wave where oscillations are perpendicular to the direction of energy transfer.
A wave where oscillations are parallel to the direction of energy transfer.
The distance from one point on a wave to the identical corresponding point on the next wave.
The number of complete wave cycles passing a fixed point per second, measured in hertz.
The bouncing of waves off a surface where the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection.
The change in direction and speed of waves when passing from one medium into another.
The spreading out of waves as they pass through an aperture or around an obstacle.

mistakes.w: Connecting an ammeter in parallel across a component.
mistakes.r: Ammeters must always be connected in series with the component to measure the current passing through it.

mistakes.w: Stating that frequency changes when water waves refract.
mistakes.r: Frequency remains constant during refraction because it is set by the wave source.

mistakes.w: Saying adding resistors in series decreases total resistance.
mistakes.r: Adding resistors in series increases total resistance because the path is longer and harder to navigate.

mistakes.w: Forgetting to measure across multiple wavelengths in standing wave experiments.
mistakes.r: Always measure across several loops or wavelengths to reduce percentage uncertainty.

mistakes.w: Confusing transverse and longitudinal wave oscillation directions.
mistakes.r: Transverse oscillations are perpendicular; longitudinal oscillations are parallel.

mistakes.w: Leaving the power supply switched on continuously during resistance practicals.
mistakes.r: Switch off between readings to prevent component heating, which changes resistance values.

mistakes.w: Failing to state that the angle of incidence is measured from the normal.
mistakes.r: Angles must always be measured relative to the normal line, not the surface boundary.

exam.q: Describe how to set up an electrical circuit to find the resistance of an unknown resistor.
model: Connect a power supply in series with an ammeter and the unknown resistor.
Connect a voltmeter in parallel across the unknown resistor.
Record readings of current from the ammeter and potential difference from the voltmeter.
Calculate resistance using R = V / I.
exam.tip: Always specify meter placement clearly: ammeter in series, voltmeter in parallel.

exam.q: Explain why the total resistance decreases when another resistor is added in parallel.
model: Adding a resistor in parallel provides an additional branch for charge to flow.
This increases the total current drawn from the supply for the same potential difference, lowering resistance.
exam.tip: Mention alternative paths and increased total current.

exam.q: A ripple tank is used to study water waves. Describe how to measure the wavelength of the waves.
model: Use a stroboscope to freeze the wave pattern or take a photograph with a ruler in the tank.
Measure the distance across multiple wave crests using the ruler.
Divide the measured distance by the number of waves to find a single wavelength.
exam.tip: Always divide by the number of waves when measuring multiple lengths to reduce error.

exam.q: Explain what happens to the speed, frequency, and wavelength of water waves when they move from deep water into shallow water.
model: Speed decreases as the waves enter shallow water.
Frequency remains constant because it is determined by the source.
Wavelength decreases since v = f * lambda and speed drops while frequency is constant.
Wavefronts change direction (refract) if entering at an angle.
exam.tip: Remember frequency never changes across medium boundaries.

model: The angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection.

exam.q: Describe how diffraction of water waves changes when the gap size in a barrier is made much larger than the wavelength.
model: Little diffraction occurs.
Wavefronts pass straight through with only slight bending at the edges of the gap.
exam.tip: Contrast this with maximum diffraction when gap size equals wavelength.

exam.q: Calculate the resistance of a component when the potential difference is 6.0 V and the current is 0.25 A.
model: R = V / I
exam.tip: State the formula, substitute values, and include unit ohms.

exam.q: Explain how a student can reduce random errors when measuring current in a circuit.
model: Take repeated measurements of current for each setting.
Calculate a mean average value.
exam.tip: Repeating and averaging is the standard method for reducing random errors.

exam.q: Describe the difference between transverse and longitudinal waves with examples.
model: Transverse waves have oscillations perpendicular to energy transfer (e.g., light, water ripples).
Longitudinal waves have oscillations parallel to energy transfer (e.g., sound waves).
Both transfer energy without transferring matter.
exam.tip: Give both the definition and a correct example for full marks.

worked.q: Water waves in a ripple tank have a frequency of 10 Hz and a wavelength of 0.05 m. Calculate their wave speed.
steps: State the wave equation: v = f * lambda.

worked.q: A student measures the potential difference across a resistor as 4.5 V and the current flowing through it as 0.15 A. Calculate the resistance.
steps: State Ohm's Law formula for resistance: R = V / I.
